items.name: Printing press
clues: The people whose job was to copy books by hand.
Ideas could spread faster and further than ever before, and books got much cheaper.
Mainz, on the Rhine, in the middle of the 15th century.
A goldsmith called Johannes Gutenberg, who used small letters made of metal that could be moved around and used again.
His most famous book was a Bible. Only around fifty copies survive, and they're worth millions.
A machine that presses ink onto paper.

items.name: Steam engine
clues: Anyone who did heavy work with their muscles, or with horses.
It powered factories, mines, trains and ships, and started the Industrial Revolution.
Earlier versions pumped water out of English mines, but the big improvement came from a workshop at the University of Glasgow.
James Watt, from Greenock in Scotland, who patented a separate condenser in 1769 and later went into business with Matthew Boulton in Birmingham.
A unit of power is named after the inventor: you'll find it on every light bulb.
It runs on boiling water.

items.name: Assembly line
clues: Skilled workers who used to build a whole product themselves.
Each worker did one small task again and again, and the work came to them.
A factory in Highland Park, near Detroit, in 1913.
Henry Ford.
Building one Model T went from about twelve and a half hours to about an hour and a half.
A line where parts are put together as they move past the workers.

items.name: Shipping container
clues: Dockworkers, who used to load and unload ships by hand, one sack or crate at a time.
Moving goods around the world became so cheap that it made globalisation possible.
A ship sailed from Newark, near New York, to Houston in April 1956 with 58 of them on board.
Malcom McLean, an American lorry-company owner who was tired of waiting at the docks.
Today the biggest ships can carry more than twenty thousand of them. People also turn them into cafés and student flats.
A big steel box that fits on a ship, a train or a lorry.

items.name: Barcode
clues: Shop staff who stuck a price label on every item and typed every price into the till.
Shops could suddenly know exactly what they had sold and what they had left.
The idea came on a beach in Miami, when the inventor drew dots and dashes from Morse code in the sand and pulled them down into lines.
Norman Woodland and Bernard Silver patented it in 1952, but the technology to read it took another twenty years.
The first product ever scanned at a checkout was a pack of Juicy Fruit chewing gum, in Ohio, in June 1974.
Black and white stripes on almost everything you buy.

items.name: Spreadsheet
clues: Clerks and accountants who added up long columns of numbers by hand.
It turned the personal computer from a hobby into a serious business tool.
A student at Harvard Business School watched a professor change one number in a table on the blackboard and then rub out and rewrite everything that depended on it.
Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston, whose program came out for the Apple II in 1979.
It was the first “killer app”: people bought the computer just to run it. Microsoft's best-known version came out in 1985.
Rows, columns and cells, like Excel or Google Sheets.
